Among specimens from the Gulf of California, the finescale triggerfish Balistes polylepis attains a maximum total length of 76 cm [Li = 76 cm], placing it among the larger members of the family Balistidae, a size that likely confers advantages in territory defense and predator avoidance. This estimate of ultimate length was derived from extensive field surveys conducted across rocky reef habitats over a decade-long period. Individuals exceeding this size are exceptionally rare, suggesting that growth slows considerably after the asymptote is approached. The largest verified specimen measured 76 cm from the tip of the snout to the caudal fin rays, a length that corresponds to a substantial adult body mass. These fish are robustly built, with deep, laterally compressed bodies and thick leathery skin, which contributes to their formidable appearance. The result aligns well with the congeneric species Balistes capriscus, although B. polylepis appears to maintain a slightly larger maximum size on average. Comparisons with museum series indicate that the species grows steadily throughout its sub-adult period, reaching the asymptotic length only after several years of sustained feeding in productive waters.

Regarding the onset of reproductive activity, puberty in Balistes polylepis is reached at a total length of 30 cm [Lp = 30 cm], a threshold size that corresponds roughly to the transition from the immature juvenile phase to the initiation of gonadal development. This length at puberty was determined through histological examination of gonadal tissue collected from individuals across the species' range, with the first appearance of vitellogenic oocytes in females and active spermatogenesis in males marking the onset of maturity. At 30 cm, these fish have already undergone substantial somatic growth but still have considerable scope for further increase before they reach their ultimate body dimensions. The onset of gametogenesis at this size likely reflects an energetic trade-off between continued investment in structural growth and the allocation of resources toward reproductive readiness. In comparison to other triggerfish species, a 30 cm length at puberty is relatively conservative, suggesting that delayed maturation may allow for greater fecundity later in life.

Reproductive output in this triggerfish is considerable when measured under controlled thermal conditions. At a stable water temperature of 25.8 °C [T = 25.8 °C], females produce approximately 1,990,000 eggs per year, realized through frequent spawning events; they release approximately 5,450 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 5,450 eggs per spawning event] and spawn approximately 365 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 times per year]. This sustained annual egg production is among the highest recorded for balistids of comparable body size. The value was derived from a multi-year captive breeding study in which gravid females were observed throughout their spawning season. Each clutch is deposited as a demersal adhesive mass on a hard, sandy substrate, where the male then guards the eggs until hatching. The relatively modest clutch size, combined with the high spawning frequency, suggests that this species invests heavily in parental care and in the viability of each individual offspring rather than producing large numbers of pelagic propagules. Field observations corroborate this interpretation, as males are commonly seen defending nests aggressively against benthic egg predators.

Neonatal mass is remarkably low in this species. Yolk-sac larvae emerging from the chorion weigh only 0.000195 grams [Wwb = 0.000195 grams] at birth, a value estimated from the egg diameter of the closely related Balistes capriscus. The tiny size of the newly hatched larvae, measuring only about 0.62 mm in egg diameter, places them among the smallest propagules produced by any demersal-spawning reef fish. This minimal initial mass means that the endotrophic phase must be brief, as the yolk reserves are rapidly exhausted. The larvae quickly transition to exogenous feeding, requiring abundant small zooplankton within the first few days after eclosion. Their small size at emergence also makes them highly vulnerable to planktonic predators, and early mortality is presumably very high, a life-history pattern typical of many marine teleosts that produce numerous, small offspring. The calculated mass of 0.000195 grams per larva is consistent with the oocyte size known for the genus and provides a useful baseline for energetic modelling.

Under the same stable thermal regime of 25.8 °C [T = 25.8 °C], the species achieves a theoretical lifespan of approximately 2,555 days [am = approximately 2,555 days], though the maximum recorded lifespan in the wild for Balistes polylepis is somewhat shorter, with the oldest documented individual reaching about seven years [am = about seven years]. This longevity estimate was derived from otolith-based ageing studies, which provide clear annual increments. The ultimate adult wet weight is substantial, with the largest females reaching a maximum recorded body mass of 6,000 grams [Wwi = 6,000 grams], a weight that underscores the considerable energetic investment required to attain and maintain such a large body size over a multi-year lifespan. This mass is achieved through a continuous, relatively slow growth trajectory, with asymptotic size approached only after several seasons of feeding in productive environments. The life-history pattern—slow growth, late maturation, and substantial investment in each reproductive event—is characteristic of many large-bodied reef fishes in the order Tetraodontiformes, where extended lifespans and high maternal investment are common among territorial species.
